title: The largest power of two in a remainder predicts both primes on 36,696,721
impact: The remainder after subtracting 6,057² is 9,472. Its power-of-two part is 256. Adding 256 to twice the root gives the prime sum 12,370 and the factors 4,937 and 7,433.
scope: Constructed example. One discriminant square test verifies the prediction. Ordinary consecutive Fermat takes 128 midpoint tests.
detail: Two other products have the identical remainder 138. One prediction succeeds and the other misses.

title: Of 12,356 correct guesses, only 523 reached the primes sooner
impact: Trying the predicted midpoint first saved 1,009 exact square tests on hits and added 1,881 on misses, for 872 extra tests overall.
scope: All 228,713 unordered pairs of distinct 14-bit primes with a 28-bit product. The baseline screens for parity and square residues modulo 256.
detail: Missed guesses are skipped on fallback. At each of the six widths from 9 to 14 the change increased the total number of exact square tests.

sources.label: How the order changes the search

title: Even every possible shift covers fewer than one in 2^482 full-size inputs
impact: A positive integer shift works exactly when the missing amount in the prime sum divides the square-root remainder. Counting every possible shift bounds the reach of the whole family.
scope: All distinct 1,024-bit prime pairs with a 2,048-bit product. The bound gives the search every divisor of the remainder for free.
detail: For p < q ≤ H at most 12H√H + 2H pairs admit any shift. Giving away the factors on every such full-size pair would save less than one part in 2^434 of the screened Fermat search’s exact square tests.

title: Free factors on every square-remainder hit would save less than one part in 2^439
impact: Even skipping every exact square test on those hits saves less than this fraction of the baseline work across all eligible full-size pairs.
scope: Distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. Work counts exact square tests in the parity- and modulo-256-screened Fermat search.
detail: More than two thirds of pairs have prime gaps large enough for at least 2^977 distinct midpoints to pass the baseline screen.

sources.label: From input frequency to search work

title: Why a stronger midpoint stride can skip lookups while keeping every square test
impact: Inside the known step-four class, checking squares modulo 16 or 32 already forces the sharper step of eight or sixteen. A modulo-256 screen therefore sends exactly the same candidates to the square test.
scope: Applies after the product has supplied the correct step-four class. The required smaller modulus depends on the product modulo eight.
detail: On 525,689 and 133,901 the next smaller power-of-two screen admits a wrong midpoint before the true one.

title: A square-remainder test saved 2,675 exact square tests and took 2.49% longer
impact: The rule used 4,678,930 exact square tests against the modulo-256 baseline’s 4,681,605, a 0.0571% reduction. It added 363,054 small lookups overall.
scope: All 228,713 distinct 14-bit prime pairs with a 28-bit product. At widths 9 through 13 the rule also cost more exact square tests than the baseline.
detail: In five paired runs on CPython 3.9.6, Darwin arm64, median elapsed time per cohort rose from 0.909 to 0.931 seconds and median process CPU time from 0.904 to 0.927 seconds. Elapsed time increased in all five pairs, with a median increase of 2.49% and a range of 1.49% to 3.64%.

title: Fewer than one in 2^487 full-size products passes the remainder test
impact: On a hit, the product is a sum of squares whose smaller coordinate is below 2^513. Counting these coordinates and their possible partners bounds the fraction.
scope: All distinct 1,024-bit prime pairs with a 2,048-bit product. The bound uses an elementary prime count.
detail: Trying up to 2^40 fixed coordinates of this size covers fewer than one in 2^960 eligible pairs.

title: A public square remainder narrows the search on 525,689
impact: Subtracting 725² leaves 64. Its square root certifies a congruence that reaches 521 × 1,009 on the fifth midpoint test. Ordinary Fermat takes 40.
scope: Selected for its two-squares representation. Against a modulo-256 screen, both searches take three exact square tests once the remainder test is counted.
detail: The shortcut can miss a representable product. For 8,249 the remainder is 149, even though 8,249 is 32² + 85².

title: The sign at the imaginary unit selects a sum remainder modulo 16 or 32
impact: When the product is 1 modulo 4, the two possible readings select the positive or negative of N+1. The modulus is 32 for N equal to 5 modulo 8 and 16 otherwise.
scope: The reading is supplied, or a two-squares representation certifies the negative imaginary value. The sharpness proof compares unit pairs with the same product residue.
detail: The products 9,017 and 8,249 share eight low bits and have opposite readings. Their sums are 6 and 10 modulo 16.

title: One complex angle gives the whole prime sum
impact: For balanced factors, the angle of a supplied polynomial value divided by its conjugate gives the sum directly. At target size, reading error below 2^-1025 still uniquely identifies it.
scope: The formula uses the principal angle at a specified root. The noisy comparison uses exact candidate phases. A cheap full-size acquisition remains open.
detail: On six toy inputs, constructing the polynomial took 8,432–14,588 trial divisions. Its degree already gave the sum.

title: Seven is the first modulus where the mean square can add a new bit
impact: Two products equal to 1 modulo 7 have mean squares 6 and 4. At 7 the bit tests whether the sum or gap is divisible by 7, with the product choosing which question applies.
scope: For unit pairs, the equal-or-opposite test is fixed by the product remainder for all pairs exactly at divisors of 24 and the two additional moduli 5 and 10.
detail: At product remainder 3, the value distinguishes the sum divisible by 7 at 9,523 from the sum at 11,413.

sources.label: Four exact controls and both means

title: The mean square is six for about a third of full-size pairs in each product class modulo 7
impact: At each nonzero product remainder the fraction is within 1/17,010 of one third using published unconditional bounds for primes in arithmetic progressions.
scope: All unordered pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The published endpoint estimates enter the Lean calculation as explicit premises.
detail: An elementary count gives more than one in 36 across the whole population. Under the Dirichlet-GRH estimate the error in each class is at most 2/(9 × 2^480).

title: A shared correction still fails through 5,500 times the lower prime bound
impact: At each cutoff through 5,500 × 2^1023, two eligible products defeat every choice of one shared scale factor for the truncated reading. By 5,768 × 2^1023 the raw sum already guarantees the decoder’s tolerance.
scope: The correction can depend on word size and cutoff. The proof covers a common additive correction to the logarithm, equivalently a common positive multiplier of the reading, in exact arithmetic.
detail: The two products share their larger prime. At the small cutoff 31, the same incompatibility already holds for 551 and 667.

title: Even summing through degree 2^1034 exceeds the certified error tolerance
impact: A series calculated from the product alone can supply the reading that identifies the prime sum. At 1,024-bit factor size, every cutoff through 2^1034 misses the decoder’s sufficient tolerance.
scope: The bounds cover direct truncation in exact arithmetic. Summing through degree 5,768 × 2^1023 guarantees the tolerance. An individual input may still decode with a larger error.
detail: A dense scan reaches the smaller prime and discovers it by gcd before reaching either cutoff. Estimating the omitted tail would need a separate error bound.

sources.label: The series and its two cutoffs
Proof using only the public product

title: The square-root estimate meets the tolerance on fewer than one in 2^500 products
impact: The share is also greater than one in 2^517. The proof counts all pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, with each unordered pair counted once.
scope: This bounds how often substituting the square root for both unknown primes attains the decoder’s stated tolerance. The proof is unconditional.
detail: The lower bound counts nearby primes sharing a short interval. For the upper bound, each possible larger prime has only a limited number of partners close enough to qualify.

title: Whenever the square-root estimate meets the tolerance, Fermat’s first test also succeeds
impact: For 10,403, the estimate meets the tolerance and the first midpoint, 102, gives 101 × 103. For 551, the first midpoint gives 19 × 29 but the estimate misses.
scope: The implication holds for distinct balanced odd prime factors. The examples were chosen to show that Fermat can succeed on the first test in either case.
detail: A squared gap of at most B/16 guarantees the tolerance when both primes lie between B and 2B. The gap between 101 and 103 attains that threshold at B = 64.

title: Every nonzero logarithmic coefficient below the product already gives a prime
impact: For 551, the coefficients at indices 18, 38, and 58 are 0, 19, and 29. Each nonzero value is just the greatest common divisor of its index and 551.
scope: The identity holds for the logarithmic derivative of the measured polynomial at every positive index below a product of two distinct primes. At a multiple of the product, the coefficient is the prime sum.
detail: If a finite weighted sum of such coefficients is nonzero, at least one sampled index already gives a prime by gcd. For 32,881 every index from 1 through 128 gives zero.

title: A dense Taylor scan needs over 2^1024 positions to get even constant accuracy
impact: At the rational measurement point, stopping the polynomial before degree p+q leaves absolute error at least 1/18. Including that degree gives the exact reading.
scope: This counts consecutive coefficient positions starting at zero for distinct 1,024-bit prime factors. Other evaluation methods have separate costs.
detail: At any pair of opposite points, the projection of every shorter Taylor prefix is exactly zero for odd primes. For 551 the cutoff is degree 48.

title: One bounded reading distinguishes every feasible prime sum
impact: For balanced 1,024-bit factors, a supplied polynomial value rounded to 1,035 fractional bits uniquely identifies the integer sum.
scope: The value is at a real point determined by the word size. The proof compares exact trial values over all real factor pairs in the size interval, including nearly equal factors.
detail: On a curve of fixed product, changing the sum by one changes the value by at least 1/(2592B), where B is the lower word bound. A cheap method to acquire this value from the product remains open.

title: A single reading of 32,881 distinguishes sums 370 and 382
impact: The reading is between 0.026104 and 0.026105. The false sum 370 predicts more than 0.026248. The true sum 382 gives 131 and 251.
scope: Both sums pass the stated screens modulo 16, 3, 5 and 7. A screen modulo 11 already rules out 370. Direct Fermat search uses ten midpoint tests.
detail: The independent polynomial construction uses 33,260 trial divisions and encounters both factors before measuring. The receipt also contains the separate 551 control.

title: Two rational readings give a decoder with a counted cost
impact: After receiving two values rounded to 1,029 fractional bits, at most 1,026 comparisons recover the sum of two distinct 1,024-bit primes.
scope: The bound starts when both readings are available. Each power comparison needs at most 2,052 rounded multiplications of operands no wider than 2,059 bits.
detail: Averaging evaluations at opposite points cancels the individual prime powers. At 551, six comparisons identify sum 48. Parity also identifies that sum on this control.

title: The first nonnegative inverse cyclotomic coefficient is the smaller prime
impact: At most 1,023 supplied coefficient signs locate the smaller of two distinct 1,024-bit primes. The ordinary cyclotomic polynomial has nonzero coefficients at the odd prime positions in the factor band.
scope: A sign costs a query to the inverse polynomial. Finding those signs cheaply from the product remains open. Directly checking all the odd ordinary coefficients takes 2^1022 positions.
detail: The binary inverse polynomial has one negative block and one positive block. For the ordinary polynomial, a weighted sum through the square root returns the smaller prime.

title: Small adaptive probes usually miss the informative ordinary coefficients
impact: Even with a 64-bit product tag and up to 2^64 adaptive coefficient or prefix-sum probes, fewer than one in 2^879 eligible products gives a nonzero reply in the factor band.
scope: The tag selects a strategy. Later queries may depend on earlier answers. The model limits further access to product-specific information when choosing the indices.
detail: A separate bound allows up to 2^128 fixed offsets from the public square root. Fewer than one in 2^877 eligible prime pairs meets a prime-dependent position at those offsets.

title: Among prime pairs that pass the square test, fewer than one in 2^979 are rotations
impact: More than one in 393,217 eligible prime pairs passes the test even though neither prime is a binary rotation of the other.
scope: All unordered pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product receive equal weight. The bound holds without any assumption that the primes' square classes are uniformly distributed.
detail: After fixing the square class at three, 15 yes-or-no answers suffice to classify each prime. Two primes with matching answers give a product that passes. The number of such pairs dwarfs the upper bound on true rotations.

sources.label: Why actual prime products must give false positives

title: The product modulo three determines the parity of a binary rotation
impact: A remainder of one allows 511 even nonzero shifts between 1,024-bit words. A remainder of two allows 512 odd shifts.
scope: This relation assumes one factor is a cyclic rotation of the other. Each prime must exceed three and the word width must be even.
detail: Rotating a word multiplies its residue by a power of two modulo one less than the next power of two. At even widths this modulus is divisible by three.

sources.label: Parity formula and exact shift counts

title: The modular rotation test accepts one in 32,768 unit residues
impact: At the public modulus 2^1,024 − 1, a passing square test has exactly 65,536 possible roots. The two passing classes of inputs are disjoint.
scope: The exact fraction counts all residues coprime to the public modulus with equal weight. The separate prime-pair result bounds the frequency among products of actual primes.
detail: Lean checks all sixteen distinct prime factors of the public modulus. In the separate six-bit census, six of fourteen prime products pass a square test. Four are actual rotations and two are false positives.

sources.label: Exact factorization of the public constant

title: Fewer than one in 2^998 eligible prime pairs are binary rotations
impact: Allowing all 1,023 nonzero shifts still covers fewer than one in 2^998 pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product.
scope: Each eligible unordered prime pair counts once. The shift may vary with the product. The bound is unconditional.
detail: A fixed prime has at most one partner for each shift. Every actual pair can be counted starting with either prime.

title: Two blocks reversed, plus one, give a prime pair after 14 comparisons
impact: At radix 64 the public product 10,850,303 gives block product 2,623. Of the two indices 61 and 62, only 61 reconstructs the primes 2,749 and 3,947.
scope: This control was chosen with the larger factor exactly one above the reversed smaller factor. The radix and offset are fixed when reading the product.
detail: Three binary searches exploit the increasing differences of an exact rational function. Ordinary Fermat needs 55 midpoint tests on the same input.

title: A known offset needs at most one row per unit of shift
impact: At a positive shift t and radix at most 2^k, at most 3kt rational comparisons and 2t final digit checks suffice for this shifted-reversal family.
scope: The smaller factor is Ba+b with 0<a≤b<B and the larger is Bb+a+t. Both the radix and the positive offset are supplied to the rule.
detail: Each row has at most two relevant indices, even when a target meets both sides of the same minimum. A composite example realizes both.

sources.label: Binary searches and equal neighboring minima

title: Even a choice among 2^128 offsets rarely explains a full-size pair
impact: Fewer than one in 2^361 eligible products admit any positive integer radix and a nonnegative shift through 2^128.
scope: All distinct 1,024-bit prime pairs with a 2,048-bit product count once. The chosen digits may be equal and the radix may be chosen separately for every product.
detail: For each fixed offset and radix the smaller prime already determines the larger one. Wide radices allow fewer digit choices.

title: Two square roots recover two 1,024-bit primes with exchanged blocks
impact: The formula returned both primes from their 2,048-bit product with a 512-bit block width derived from the input length. Ordinary Fermat first succeeds after more than 2^1016 tests on this product.
scope: We chose the primes to have reversed blocks and easily certified predecessors. The planted common remainder also permits a different shortcut when supplied.
detail: Both the division formula and the modular formula recover the pair in Lean. A separate replay starts with the decimal product and checks both returned primes.

sources.label: Full-size proof and exact Fermat comparison

title: Division identifies exchanged blocks even when multiplication has carries
impact: At radix 31, the quotient 515 and remainder 14 single out the block product 510. Two square roots then give the prime factors 557 and 947 of 527,479.
scope: Two positive distinct blocks appearing in opposite order in a chosen integer radix. The formula handles both odd and even radices.
detail: The quotient overestimates the block product by less than one radix, and the product gives the missing remainder.

title: Even choosing the radix separately for every product rarely exposes a reversed pair
impact: Fewer than one in 2^490 eligible products admit a two-block reversal in any integer radix. Restricting the choice to all binary widths gives fewer than one in 2^1006.
scope: All pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with 2,048-bit products, counted once. The all-radix bound allows odd radices and both digit parities.
detail: Small radices permit one partner per prime, and at large radices the allowed digits shrink. Any one pair can qualify at only one binary block width.

title: A mismatch between the ends of the product can rule out a block width
impact: At base 512 the product 43,431,077 has first and last bytes 165. Its nearby control starts with 165 and ends with 29, immediately ruling out that width.
scope: For full-size reversed-block products the test is valid at binary widths of 683 bits and above in the eligible range. Passing the screen is a necessary condition.
detail: In this range three product coefficients are small enough to occupy separate digits, and the outer coefficient appears twice.

sources.label: Bit threshold and checked hit and miss

title: Midpoint and gap divisibility turn one remainder into an integer square
impact: With fixed divisors 11 and 7, the remainder 25 gives the half-gap 35 at 37,979 and recovers 163 and 233. At 536,113 the second lift recovers 653 and 821.
scope: The examples satisfy the divisibility conditions. At fixed positive coprime divisors, the first-lift condition holds on fewer than one in 2^1007 eligible pairs.
detail: The product fixes the squared, scaled half-gap modulo the square of the midpoint divisor. Its exact quotient gives the lift index.

sources.label: Coverage of a fixed pair of divisors

title: Reversing three blocks gives at most two readings when the digits multiply without a carry
impact: At radix 61 the only triple for 172,659,841 gives primes 11,411 and 15,131. A composite control admits two genuinely different pairs.
scope: The central coefficient a²+b²+c² must be less than the radix. At least one prime factor suffices for uniqueness within the family.
detail: The outer product digits give the sum and difference of two hidden quantities via square roots. Checking the two ways to assign them takes at most two further roots.

sources.label: Exact candidate count, primality and controls

title: Rounding a ratio of polynomials rarely gives the prime sum
impact: With numerator and denominator degrees up to 2^28, even unlimited coefficients give fewer than one exact hit in 2^453 products. The fraction within 2^128 is below one in 2^388.
scope: One fixed ratio, rounded down to an integer. Every eligible full-size pair counts once. A zero denominator counts as a miss.
detail: The poles and zeros of the derivative cut the number line into a limited number of pieces. On each piece rounding preserves the direction of the prediction.

sources.label: What a change of direction allows

title: Five larger products give five smaller prime sums
impact: From 32,881 through 34,427, the sums decrease from 382 to 372. A sequence longer than 2^979 exists among 2,048-bit products.
scope: All five small examples use eight-bit primes. The large result proves existence among full-size pairs whose primes differ by at least 2^1006.
detail: Sort by product and take sums in that order. Every later sum on the selected sequence is strictly smaller.

sources.label: Five pairs and the full-size theorem

title: An always-increasing or flat guess almost never gives the prime sum
impact: Even the best nondecreasing prediction is exact on fewer than one in 2^484 products. Allowing an error of 2^128 still gives fewer than one in 2^419.
scope: Every distinct pair of 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product counts once. The prediction can use the entire product and unlimited computation.
detail: The proof counts the product blocks and sum values the prediction can reach, then bounds the number of pairs in each cell.

title: On more than two thirds of the products, widely separated primes sharpen the limit
impact: Within the group whose primes differ by at least 2^1006, a nondecreasing prediction is exact on fewer than one in 2^979. The fraction within 2^128 is below one in 2^850.
scope: Each rate uses the separated group as its denominator. The proof that this group exceeds two thirds of all eligible pairs is unconditional.
detail: For a fixed sum, two separated pairs give products too far apart to share a block of width 2^1006.

sources.label: Gap count, spacing and hit rates

title: Twice the rounded-up square root reaches a provable share of prime sums
impact: This explicit prediction is exact on more than one in 2^516 eligible products and comes within 2^128 on more than one in 2^452.
scope: Each result counts all eligible distinct 1,024-bit prime pairs. The close pairs supply a lower bound on how often the rule works.
detail: Primes that share a sufficiently short interval give a midpoint near the square root of their product. A prime count forces many such pairs.

sources.label: The explicit prediction and both bounds

title: A prediction that only falls or stays level gets even fewer sums right
impact: The exact sum agrees on fewer than one in 2^1007 eligible products. At fixed smaller prime, at most one partner can agree exactly.
scope: A single nonincreasing natural-number prediction over all eligible full-size pairs.
detail: Increasing the larger prime increases both the true sum and product. With error E, at most 2E+1 partners for each smaller prime can fit.

title: A multiplier chosen from 697 turns a silent sphere count into the prime 41
impact: Multipliers 1 and 2 at 697 repeat public baselines. The Jacobi sign test picks 10. The large count 18,696 divided by the base count 24 gives 779, enough to recover 41.
scope: The small counts were independently enumerated. The general identity uses the classical three-square recurrence. Computing the large count cheaply remains open.
detail: For a represented positive multiplier of negative Jacobi sign, the normalized large count equals the product plus twice one of its primes.

title: The RH connection bounds an informative three-square multiplier by 4,030,330
impact: Given the external least-prime estimate, a small prime of negative Jacobi symbol exists at most 2,015,165. A multiplier at most twice that bound always gives a count sensitive to a prime.
scope: Distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The local theorem takes the least-prime estimate, the three-square existence theorem, and the representation recurrence as explicit premises.
detail: The multiplier can be selected by Jacobi symbols computed from the product alone. An accurate count for the resulting much larger target must still be obtained.

title: At 697 an estimate less than 48 away would still identify 41
impact: For a mixed-sign multiplier with base count b, an absolute error strictly below 2b determines the selected prime. If the error bound is ε, all compatible candidate primes are within ε/b of one another.
scope: A positive base count and an error guarantee on the supplied large count are required. The rounding bound uses the oddness of the prime.
detail: At a base count of 6, the midpoint between readings for the abstract odd candidates 5 and 7 shows why the strict half-spacing cannot be relaxed solely by the rounding argument.

title: The square-root census counts every ordered signed integer triple exactly once
impact: Lean proves that the signed integer-triple count and this project's three-square count agree for every target, including zero. The positive-target external recurrence then implies the project's all-target recurrence.
scope: The census equality is unconditional. The recurrence implication takes the external positive-target theorem as an input. Its upstream proof uses another Lean version.
detail: At zero the origin contributes one. The adapter handles the division branch and the change between Jacobi and Legendre symbols at an odd prime.

sources.label: Upstream sources and local proof scope

title: Averaging the modular counts by Jacobi sign erases the factor-sensitive displacement
impact: At N=15 the positive-sign counts 120 and 360 average to 240. The negative-sign counts 180 and 240 average to 210. For every such product the mean is N(N+J), already computable.
scope: Uniform coprime ternary targets with fixed Jacobi sign J for a product of two distinct odd primes. The variance still depends on the sum or the gap.
detail: Both supported counts occur equally often. Their variance is N² times the square of the prime sum for positive sign and times the square of the prime gap for negative sign.

title: A fixed polynomial equation of degree 2¹²⁸ covers fewer than one in 2⁸⁷⁹ full-size products
impact: Every eligible pair counts as a hit whenever its true sum satisfies the equation, even if thousands of wrong sums also satisfy it.
scope: One fixed nonzero rational polynomial in the product and the sum. The count is unconditional over all pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes giving a 2,048-bit product.
detail: Substitution of pq and p+q preserves nonvanishing. A finite-grid root bound and unconditional estimates for the number of eligible pairs give the stated share.

title: The best quadratic on ten small semiprimes covers seven and encodes two primes
impact: From 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13, every quadratic covering seven of the ten products accepts exactly the pairs containing two preselected entries.
scope: On an n-entry grid the exact number of distinct pairs covered at degree d ≤ n−1 is bounded by the number touching d entries. The equality classification requires d < n−1.
detail: A degree-two example encodes 3 and 5. It accepts the sum 16 on product 55 and misses the sum 24 on 143.

title: Choosing the equation after seeing the whole product has a degree budget
impact: Up to 2³² preselected polynomials of degree at most 2⁹⁶ still cover fewer than one in 2⁸⁷⁹ eligible products, even when any rule chooses among them.
scope: The finite collection is fixed in advance. The selection may use the entire input, and the bound even grants credit if any entry fits.
detail: Multiply all the nonzero equations to obtain a single nonzero polynomial. Its degree is at most the sum of the degrees. Clearing a nonvanishing denominator also puts an exact rational prediction in this class.

title: A window of 2¹²⁸ either side still rarely contains the prime sum
impact: For an integer polynomial of degree at most 2³², even allowing this much error leaves fewer than one hit in 2⁸⁴⁵ eligible products.
scope: Exactly evaluated, fixed integer-coefficient predictions. The theorem concerns the entire 2,048-bit prime-pair population.
detail: Each signed integer error corresponds to a shifted polynomial equation. Multiplying them accounts for the entire window. The example 20 ± 2 contains the sums on 77 and 85, and misses 143.

title: A scale-invariant quadratic can fit just one distinct semiprime across all sizes
impact: If every term of a polynomial scales the same way when both primes are rescaled, degree d permits at most floor(d/2) distinct prime pairs. A family of equations attains this bound.
scope: Fixed nonzero rational equations, with weight two on the product and one on the sum. The primes are distinct and counted without order.
detail: The reduced denominator of the sum squared divided by the product is exactly the product. The pair 7 and 11 gives 324/77, uniquely. Each root of the normalized equation therefore gives at most one semiprime.

title: A count of 360 triples modulo 15 gives the prime sum 8
impact: For every product N of two distinct odd primes, the number of triples whose squares add to −1 modulo N is N(p+1)(q+1). Divide by N and subtract N+1 to get the sum.
scope: The point count is supplied. Obtaining it cheaply from one large product remains open. No relationship between the prime sizes is required.
detail: For any target coprime to N, the public Jacobi symbol specifies whether the count yields the prime sum or the prime gap. At 15, target 1 has 180 triples and yields the gap 2.

title: Extra digits of a coprime target only rescale the count
impact: Changing the modulus from N to N² multiplies every coprime-target count by exactly N². Choosing any of the N higher target digits gives the same count.
scope: Products of distinct odd primes. Targets sharing a divisor with N follow different rules.
detail: At modulus 225 the counts for targets 0, 15, 1 and 3 are 71,775, 43,200, 40,500 and 36,000. Lean accounts for each possible divisibility class at both local primes.

title: The missing slopes on a projective line count the prime sum plus one
impact: There are N ordinary slopes. Of the remaining points, p are infinite only at q, q are infinite only at p, and one is infinite at both. Counting these points would give p+q+1.
scope: The proof uses the product of the two local projective lines. Computing the size of these parts quickly with only N remains open.
detail: At N=15 there are 24 points altogether. The 9 outside the ordinary slopes consist of groups of sizes 3, 5 and 1.

sources.label: Chinese remainder chart and its complement

title: One modular circle carries the entire primitive sphere count
impact: For every coprime target, six times the number of pairs of squares representing it modulo N equals the primitive sphere count at radius N. At 15 there are 16 circle points and 96 primitive sphere points.
scope: Modulo a product of distinct odd primes, equality of all coprime-target circle counts is unconditional. The comparison to integer sphere points uses a classical sphere-count formula.
detail: Trying another coprime target repeats the same measurement. The proof checks that target zero can give a different count, 9 at modulus 15.

title: Counting triples modulo N² gives the sum for every balanced prime pair
impact: For 35 the count is 1,953,875. Dividing by 35³, rounding down, subtracting 35 and adding two yields the prime sum 12.
scope: Distinct odd primes 5 ≤ p < q ≤ 2p, including every pair of distinct 1,024-bit primes. Obtaining the count cheaply at large size remains open.
detail: The rule gives 18 at 77. At 65 the larger prime exceeds twice the smaller, and the rule gives 17 while the true sum is 18.

title: At modulus N, restricting which triples count reveals the prime sum
impact: There are exactly N² solutions in total. If P counts only triples whose coordinates together are coprime to N, then (N+1)² − P is the square of the prime sum.
scope: Products of distinct odd primes of any sizes. The primitive count is an additional measurement.
detail: At 35 the primitive count is 1,152. Subtracting it from 36² gives 144, the square of 12.

title: An error of half a cube still permits exact recovery of the sum
impact: An integer estimate within N³/2 of the true modular count determines the exact even prime sum S. The public estimate N⁴ misses by more than N³(S−2).
scope: For distinct odd primes 5 ≤ p < q ≤ 2p. The error tolerance is absolute, while the count itself is larger than N⁴.
detail: The allowed error follows from the distance between the count intervals for successive even sums. The relative error of the simple estimate N⁴ is below 3/p when measured against N⁴.

sources.label: Recovering the sum with an estimate

title: Sampling triples uniformly cannot measure the count at a modest budget
impact: For budgets from one draw through N²/4, the usual estimate from the hit rate has at least 100% relative error on every sample.
scope: The deterministic error bound concerns the ordinary hit-rate estimator. For independent uniform draws, the chance of any hit in B draws is below 2B/N².
detail: The first positive estimate is already at least twice the true count. At 15, a single uniform draw hits with exact probability 319/50,625.

title: A formal RH consequence gives an explicit small-prime witness bound
impact: For a product of two 1,024-bit primes, the outside-subgroup prime from the upper bound (log N)² is at most 2,015,165.
scope: The bound locates a small prime outside a specified proper subgroup. It does not identify an unknown factor. The separate direct gcd theorem needs a divisibility condition that fails for same-width prime pairs.
detail: An external Lean 4.36 project proves the analytic result and connects it to the released Dirichlet theorem. This Lean 4.19 library verifies the input conditions and integer conversion with the analytic statement supplied.

impact: For the seven odd primes through 19, sorting saves work in 126 patterns. The smallest positive saving is 180 lookups per full period and the largest is 2,992,699.
scope: Uniform phases in a full period, equal cost per lookup and a product coprime to all seven primes. Each pattern contains exactly 12,960 invertible residues.
detail: Both ties occur when the product is a nonsquare at every prime through 17. The result inventories residue classes and makes no sampling assumption about large prime factors.

title: Reordering the same 13 tests saved 3,495 lookups on the 39-bit product
impact: Sorting the public residue tables by how many residues pass reduced the scalar scan from 16,226 to 12,731 lookups. The sole survivor was again 1,310,542.
scope: One previously published product of two 20-bit primes. Both orders start with 7,273 candidates and apply the same tests to the survivors. The order uses only the small public tables.
detail: The saving is 21.54% in candidate–prime lookups. Sorting 13 fractions adds setup work. On one partial interval, interchanging two of the tests saves another 24 lookups.

title: One more reading settles the ambiguous four-position case
impact: Given all six counts and the first two tests at each position, one check of the third test identifies the joint hit or proves the window empty.
scope: Four positions with three tests and an ambiguous common count. The result supplies no inexpensive procedure for obtaining the six counts on a large interval.
detail: For w positions with k earlier tests mapped, the smallest of their groups contains at most floor(w/2ᵏ) positions. Reading that group and using the supplied margins recovers the joint count.

title: Two products give identical pair counts and different common-sum answers
impact: In the first four candidate sums, each prime test passes twice and each pair passes together once. For 10,961, one sum passes all three. For 187,709, none does.
scope: Two small semiprimes selected to compare the same residue tables at 3, 13 and 11. Both windows start at the lower end allowed by their product and balance bounds.
detail: The difference appears in the positions that pass modulo 13. Retaining the six counts alone discards this information.

title: Six counts determine the exact number of joint hits at 405 of 429 starts
impact: The counts force zero common hits in 275 windows, one in 128 and two in 2. In the 24 ambiguous windows the actual answers split evenly between zero and one.
scope: A complete period for four consecutive allowed sums when the product is 665 modulo 1,716. The percentage is over starting positions for that residue, with all six counts supplied.
detail: Sharp lower and upper bounds describe every answer consistent with three individual counts, three pair counts and the window length.

title: Every pair of tests can pass somewhere in an empty search interval
impact: On 34,387 the first three permitted sums each pass a different pair of the tests modulo 3, 13 and 11. None passes all three.
scope: A prefix at the actual lower end of this product’s balanced interval, using its public modulo-four condition. Every proper subset of the tests has a witness in that prefix.
detail: The first joint survivor is the fifth candidate, 388. Knowing just that each pair has some witness loses the positions needed to find a joint witness.

title: Remainder tests single out one full-size sum without assuming RH
impact: For any product of two 1,024-bit primes, the true sum is the only candidate in the stated public range that passes every odd prime through 2⁹⁴⁰.
scope: The proof uses the product and factor widths. It deductively applies three published unconditional inequalities, supplied as hypotheses in Lean.
detail: Visiting the entire family once would take more than 2⁹³⁰ prime visits. Finding the unique passing sum cheaply remains open.

title: The number of copies of a prime predicts its first rejecting power
impact: If d is a nonsquare modulo an odd prime and x contains that prime exactly a times, the test on d × x² first fails at exponent 2a + 1.
scope: Applies to a proposed discriminant with the stated decomposition. The example uses 9,523 = 89 × 107 and a deliberately wrong sum of 200.
detail: The example gives 1,908 = 53 × 6². Although 53 already fails modulo 3, the original discriminant passes modulo 3 and 9. It fails modulo 27.

title: Remainders through 43 recover the 39-bit factors without a clue
impact: The public width gives 7,273 possible sums after the modulo-four check. Three pass the primes through 41, and only 1,310,542 survives 43. This gives 556,559 × 753,983.
scope: One previously published seeded product of two 20-bit primes. The filters receive the product and factor width. The disclosed primes appear in the final verification.
detail: A direct staged scan uses 16,226 small remainder lookups. The Lean proof checks the complete sequence of counts with bit masks. This example establishes no success rate on larger inputs.

title: Small remainders cut the full-size sum counts about 125-fold and 84-fold
impact: Against the modulo-four count, testing the odd primes through 19 reduces the number of final square tests by a factor between 124.73 and 124.74 on the fresh control, and between 84.19 and 84.20 on the crossed control.
scope: Two published 2,048-bit products, using only each product and its factor widths. The counts cover visiting the whole allowed interval. Both have more than 2¹⁰⁰⁰ surviving sums.
detail: The proof counts complete periods and bounds the last partial period. The ratio measures the reduction in candidate count. Generating candidates and constructing small residue lists have their own costs.

title: A product-only sieve leaves at most 2⁵¹⁹ sums over the full factor-width interval
impact: Among 2¹⁰²⁴ consecutive sums covering two 1,024-bit primes, checking odd primes through 2⁵²⁰ retains the true sum and leaves at most 2⁵¹⁹ candidates.
scope: Unconditional for every pair in the stated bit widths. There are more than 2⁵¹¹ test primes. The theorem bounds survivors and leaves their efficient enumeration open.
detail: The proof specializes Gallagher’s classical larger sieve and establishes explicit finite constants for these factor-sum remainders.

title: Three prime powers allow a still coarser clue while keeping fewer than a million sums
impact: At 2,048 bits, a supplied interval total accurate to 2¹⁰⁵³ leaves at most 907,200 sums. This permits eight times the error of the earlier 635,040-candidate bound.
scope: Moduli 16, 9, 25, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. The product and factor widths give the public constraints. The estimate for the individual product remains a separate input.
detail: The combined modulus exceeds the full diameter of the possible sums at this accuracy. Each admissible residue can therefore appear at most once.

title: Small remainders let the interval clue tolerate 32 times more error
impact: An error allowance of 2¹⁰⁵⁰ leaves at most 635,040 possible sums at 2,048 bits. The previous modulo-four bound gave at most 1,048,576 at an allowance of 2¹⁰⁴⁵.
scope: Any product of two distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The remainder checks use the product alone. The interval-total estimate is supplied.
detail: Only 90,720 residues at most can be sums in a block of length 19,399,380. At this error allowance seven blocks cover every candidate, including partial blocks.

title: Remainders modulo 3 and 5 select the correct sum from five
impact: On 419,636,024,497, only 1,310,542 survives both checks. On the fresh and crossed 2,048-bit controls, the public remainders give conditional upper bounds of 272,160 and 403,200 sums.
scope: The 39-bit input used a deliberately noisy clue derived from its factors. The large-input figures assume an interval-total estimate accurate to 2¹⁰⁵⁰. No such reading was obtained on either control.
detail: Each large product determines exactly how many sum residues survive in one complete block. Multiplying that count by seven covers the possible interval.

title: Two square roots give direct access to every sum allowed by the reading
impact: For the 39-bit example the interval runs from 1,310,536 to 1,310,554. The first sum of the correct remainder is 1,310,538 and the fifth is 1,310,554.
scope: The calculation takes a supplied signed integer reading and a nonnegative error allowance. It also handles empty intervals and exact-square endpoints.
detail: Once the endpoints are known, adding four times a zero-based index to the first candidate gives the selected sum without visiting the preceding candidates.

title: Two interval readings can cancel the same unknown error
impact: On 143, adding 1,000 to both readings still recovers the prime sum 24. At 1,024-bit factor width, five publicly known lengths are always suitable for taking two readings.
scope: The measurements are supplied. If an unknown bias changes linearly with the length, every proposed sum fits the interior readings after refitting the slope and offset.
detail: A difference of totals retains a linear term in the factor sum. Two additional reference readings at lengths zero and one calibrate an affine error if that law holds globally.

title: Four gcds measure the change in slope, which is constant in the useful interval
impact: At 143 the successive measurements are −18, −22 and 2. The first two already sample gcds of 11 and 13. Inside the interval where the sum formula holds, the measurement is always 2.
scope: Four gcds of the product suffice for the second difference at every nonnegative length. The constant result applies when all three lengths include both prime contributions and lie below the smaller prime.
detail: Taking two differences cancels the linear term that carries the factor sum. The calculation pinpoints what this inexpensive product-only observation can reveal.

title: A deliberately noisy clue leaves five sums on the 39-bit example
impact: With an error allowance of 16 million, five sums remain. Only 1,310,542 gives a square discriminant and the primes 556,559 and 753,983.
scope: The disclosed factors of the seeded product 419,636,024,497 supplied the exact interval total. We added five million before giving the estimate to the sum test.
detail: The proof certifies the exact signed total, its perturbation, the full list of five candidate sums, and the resulting factorization.

title: A specified error in the interval total bounds the remaining search
impact: An absolute error of at most 2¹⁰⁴⁵ leaves at most 1,048,576 sums at 2,048 bits. At error 2¹⁰²⁵ only the correct sum survives when the estimate meets its guarantee.
scope: The decoder receives an integer estimate for the individual product. The true sum is in the list for balanced distinct odd primes.
detail: Legal sums differ by multiples of four. Their predicted totals get farther apart as the sum grows, which bounds how many can fit in one error interval.

title: A coarser supplied total can still locate the smaller prime
impact: With an estimate accurate to 2¹⁴⁵⁰, an explicit real number is within 2⁴⁷⁰ of the smaller prime except on fewer than one in 32,768 eligible pairs.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The location uses the supplied estimate, and the bound is a radius.
detail: The calculation estimates the sum first, then takes its smaller real root. The gap between the actual primes controls the loss of accuracy in this second step.

title: Even a menu of 2⁶⁴ fixed multipliers almost always misses the interval total
impact: The best prediction cN from such a menu reaches the decoding tolerance on fewer than one in 2⁴¹⁸ eligible pairs. A single coefficient reaches it on fewer than one in 2⁴⁸².
scope: Coefficients are arbitrary real numbers fixed before seeing the prime pair. The choice among menu entries can use the entire product.
detail: Each successful coefficient predicts the sum using one fixed factor ratio. Counting the larger primes that can fit around that ratio limits the coverage.

title: The complete gcd average always decodes to the wrong sum at full size when used for the short interval
impact: At 143 the substitution gives a sum of 20, while the primes add to 24. Its downward error in the interval total is at least half the squared interval length for balanced primes of size at least 11.
scope: This tests replacing the triangular interval average by the exact mean over the whole modulus. At every balanced 2,048-bit input this specific substitution fails.
detail: The complete mean has an exact divisor formula and itself contains the factor sum. Extrapolating it to the short interval introduces the error.

title: Four clues still leave at least 2⁴⁷⁴ sums after enforcing both factor widths
impact: Except on fewer than one in 4,096 eligible prime pairs, at least 2⁴⁷⁴ sums pass all four square-divisor clues with both real roots inside the exact factor-width limits.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. A second guarantee of 2¹⁸⁶ sums has an exceptional fraction below 2⁻⁴⁴.
detail: The count allows the largest possible square divisor at each sign. The roots of a surviving candidate can be nonintegral.

title: One exact character average determines the sum of the primes
impact: At 143, the even-family average is 51/25. It gives the sum 24 and the factors 11 and 13. The same formula holds for every product of distinct primes greater than eight.
scope: The input to the decoder is an exact average over primitive even Dirichlet characters. At 2,048 bits, candidate sums four apart predict averages less than 2⁻⁴⁰⁸⁷ apart.
detail: Even the size of the family determines the factors. The proof leaves open how to obtain the average cheaply from the product alone.

title: Ninety-sixth powers still cancel at the small character inputs
impact: At every even power through 96, the difference between the even and odd totals is determined entirely by the supplied weights.
scope: Two distinct 1,024-bit primes. Every character input from 1 through 2²¹ is allowed, with arbitrary complex weights. The signed totals are unnormalized.
detail: Normalization preserves a small signal. With up to 2²¹ weights, moving between two candidate sums four apart changes the predicted normalized even mean by at most 2⁻⁴⁰⁶⁷ times the total squared weight.

sources.label: Connection to the GRH input range

title: One longer character sum at a public length determines the factors
impact: On 143 the interval length is eight. Its signed total is −44, and every integer reading from −96 through 23 still gives the correct factor sum 24 after rounding.
scope: Distinct primes p < q < 2p. The interval length is the integer part of √(N/2), at least 2¹⁰²³ for a full 2,048-bit product.
detail: For a balanced 2,048-bit product, an approximation within 2¹⁰²⁵ of the exact total suffices. Obtaining such an approximation cheaply remains open.

title: Random sampling almost always misses the terms that carry the factors
impact: At 2,048 bits, even 2⁶⁴ independent draws have probability at most 2⁻⁹⁵⁸ of seeing a term that differs from one.
scope: Uniform draws with replacement from the ordered index pairs in the long character sum. At 143, ten of the 64 pairs carry a changed term.
detail: A pair changes the total only when its index sum equals p or q. Grouping by that index sum gives a direct gcd calculation with 2B−1 diagonals at interval length B.

title: Four supplied square divisors usually leave at least 2⁵¹⁴ possible sums
impact: All four clues leave at least 2⁵¹⁴ compatible sums except on a fraction below 2⁻¹³. The lower bound of 2²⁵⁸ sums holds with an exceptional fraction below 2⁻⁴⁵.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. Compatible sums pass the basic balanced interval, the true remainder modulo four, two sum congruences and two discriminant congruences.
detail: One same-sign clue leaves at least 2⁷⁶⁴ sums, or one mixed-sign clue leaves at least 2⁷⁶⁷ gaps, except on a fraction below 2⁻⁷⁷. A candidate still needs an integer square discriminant to give factors.

title: One supplied square divisor fixes the sum on a 39-bit product
impact: The sum of the factors of 419,636,024,497 must lie among 78,590 integers. Knowing that 288² divides (p+1)(q+1) leaves only 1,310,542, giving the primes 556,559 and 753,983.
scope: First seeded draw of two distinct 20-bit primes. Their disclosed factors supplied the four largest square divisors used as clues.
detail: The sum is 66,382 modulo 82,944. Exactly one integer in the balanced window has that remainder, and its discriminant is 197,424².

title: Even more guesses than possible smaller factors almost never reach a working scale
impact: Giving all four sign choices every scale through 2¹⁰²⁴ reaches fewer than one in 2⁴⁶² eligible prime pairs. A trillion-scale budget reaches fewer than one in 2⁹⁵⁹.
scope: Uniform sorted pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The bound allows product-dependent choices within the entire budget.
detail: Counting both neighboring integers together bounds how many products can be a small integer times a square. Even with a scale cap of 2¹⁷⁹² the fraction is below one in 2⁷⁷.

title: Every sign and every scale through a trillion fails on both full-size controls
impact: The fresh and crossed 2,048-bit products each have a Lean certificate ruling out all four sign choices at every positive scale through 2⁴⁰.
scope: These are retrospective checks with known factors. The fresh certificate also uses two primes disclosed by its construction.
detail: On the fresh successor product, odd prime multiplicities left 4,197 possible multipliers. Small-prime square tests ruled out all 4,197. The crossed successor product left 3,693, all excluded as well.

title: One square-root guess can test four links between the two factors
impact: On all 32,385 pairs of distinct 12-bit primes the four-sign scan found 1,343 products. The two-sign comparison found 661 on the same per-product square-root allowances.
scope: Bounded census through scale 16. Fermat found 14,500 products on matched budgets, including 14,076 missed by the four-sign scan. The four-sign scan alone found 919.
detail: The even neighbors of odd primes force an even root at every successful squarefree scale. One scaled square suffices for all four signs at scales two and above. The two readings yield either a candidate sum or a candidate gap.

title: One scaled root checks both sides of the product
impact: Across all 32,385 products of distinct 12-bit primes, trying both signs through scale 16 found 638 products. Trying the predecessor alone found 321.
scope: The candidate-selection proof applies to balanced factors. Ordinary Fermat search found 13,818 of these products on matched square-root budgets, with 463 found only by the two-sided scan.
detail: Each scale produces two possible sums. Comparing them selects the only one that can pass the balanced interval, so each scale needs at most one discriminant root. More scales can reach that last test than in the one-sided scan.

title: Two impossible factor remainders can rule out a whole family of guesses
impact: On 2,627 no squarefree multiple of 13 can be the first successful scale. Its two possible remainders modulo 169 both miss the smaller-factor interval.
scope: For a guessed prime divisor of the squarefree predecessor scale. Checking small primes saved six scaled roots on 2,627, while ordinary interval trial division found its factor in one division.
detail: The same odd-interval screen reduced 371 scaled roots to 315 on 3,713 and 524 to 483 on 4,757, in return for additional divisibility checks.

title: One weighted sum detects which prime’s sequence repeats
impact: At shift ten on 143 the first weighting incorrectly signaled a full repeat. The second weighting gave 77, whose gcd identifies 11 as the only prime with a repeat.
scope: The second weighting works for all products of distinct primes at least eleven. The calculation checks a proposed shift and still needs a full sum in the direct implementation.
detail: The first weighting has a single exceptional prime, 13. Moving the two readings one position forward and choosing coefficients 3 and −10 gives an exact test for both factors.

title: The product’s square root picks one degree that reveals a factor
impact: On 493 the chosen degree is 22. The discrepancy gives 29, and the ordinary binomial coefficient gives 17.
scope: For distinct odd primes with the larger less than twice the smaller. Computing the complete sum directly visits every residue. Twin primes have a separate square test for the coefficient method.
detail: The degree is the largest even integer at or below the square root of the product. The same discrepancy gives the larger prime at every even degree between the two prime predecessors, including the lower endpoint.

title: One weighted sum recovers the larger prime without a binomial coefficient
impact: On 2,627 the sum gave 355, which shares the factor 71 with the product. It used 2,414 modular powers in place of 4,828 for the two separate sums.
scope: The primes are at least seven, their gap is at least six and the larger is less than twice the smaller. Gaps of two and four have direct square tests.
detail: This input was chosen because the first Fermat test misses. Fermat still found 37 in three square tests, and the direct Jacobi scan had already exposed 37 on its 36th sign.

title: Two consecutive readings decide whether every later reading repeats
impact: On 119 a false shift can give the correct first value, 2, or the correct second value, 6. Getting both values certifies a repeat for the whole sequence.
scope: Every product of two distinct primes at least seven. This checks a proposed shift. Obtaining the two readings directly still takes a pass over all residues.
detail: The multipliers in the usual recurrence of consecutive middle binomial coefficients distinguish the starting position from every other interior position. The proof checks the two endpoints separately.

title: Some prime pairs give no factor from a raw even moment at any degree
impact: On 65 every positive even degree has gcd one. On 77, four degrees gave all four possible gcds, 1, 7, 11 and 77.
scope: An exact classification for distinct odd prime factors. A prime appears in the gcd precisely when it is 3 modulo 4 and one less than the prime divides the degree.
detail: The 14 control readings used 157 signs and 770 modular powers. The signs for a product were reused across its degrees.

title: On the fresh comparison the first successful scale exceeds 2¹⁰⁷⁹
impact: That first guess is larger than the smaller prime itself. On the crossed comparison the first successful scale exceeds 2⁶⁴. Both inputs exceed the trillion-guess budget.
scope: These two retrospective certificates use the published prime factors. The fresh input’s prime construction supplied two additional certified divisors. Exact first scales remain unknown.
detail: Primes occurring an odd number of times in the totient must divide every successful scale. The shortest shared periods on the fresh and crossed controls have 2,046 and 1,439 bits, respectively.

title: The product can rule out a whole class of guesses before the first square root
impact: For 3,713, its first successful scale cannot be even or divisible by 29. The product-dependent check cut the remaining scale roots from 574 to 371.
scope: The proof concerns squarefree guesses, including the first successful scale of a balanced semiprime. At 221 the check saved zero roots. Elapsed-time savings remain unmeasured.
detail: At 4,757 it reduced 740 scale roots to 524 with an additional 2,220 candidate modulus tests. Both searches used the same balanced-sum window and returned the same factor.

sources.label: When the product rules out a scale

title: A fixed table skips 36% of square-root guesses in each full block
impact: On 4,757 the same first factor appeared at guess 1,155, using 740 scale roots and 706 discriminant roots. The earlier scan used 1,155 and 1,104.
scope: The first correct scale is squarefree for balanced prime pairs. The table skips multiples of 4, 9 and 25, and works at any positive search cap.
detail: Exactly 576 of every 900 aligned guesses remain. Building the reusable table cost 2,175 small divisibility checks in the experiment.

sources.label: Lean proof of the preserved first hit

title: The distinct primes in a guessed repeat give a finite list of scales
impact: For 221 the false period guess 3 still gives a two-entry list, 1 and 3, which contains the successful square-root scale.
scope: For balanced primes, k supplied distinct prime divisors of the guess give exactly 2ᵏ scales when the list of divisors is complete. Obtaining that list has its own cost.
detail: The list contains a correct scale precisely when the squarefree part of the true shortest repeat divides the guess. The recovered pair then decides whether the guess itself repeats.

title: Two square roots and one gcd decide whether a guess is the shortest repeat
impact: Given 221, both 3 and 48 lead to the prime factors during the check. Recomputing the period rejects both guesses as the minimum and accepts 12.
scope: This exact equality test uses the product and a proposed length for two distinct primes at least seven. It takes one guess as input.
detail: A unit-power test accepts every multiple of the shortest repeat. The equality test reconstructs a candidate pair, verifies its product, and checks the exact reduced-predecessor product.

title: One square-root guess can succeed while the first period grows without bound
impact: On the constructed product 547,606,837, the very first square-root guess gives 22,501 and 24,337. The shortest shared repeat is 422,500.
scope: This is a special family with square totient. The finite formulas are checked in Lean. The infinitude argument applies a published theorem about fifty linear forms.
detail: For any prescribed period threshold, the construction admits pairs above it with q−p at least p/300. The direct calculation needs only the product and scale one.

title: A trillion square-root guesses still reach very few balanced pairs
impact: Fewer than one in 2⁷³⁶ eligible prime pairs yields its true sum at any square-root scale up to 2⁴⁰.
scope: The bound counts sorted distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. It applies to direct sum recovery, including successful guesses shorter than the first period.
detail: A successful scale forces the totient to be that scale times a square. Counting the possible square roots and divisors gives a finite estimate at the project’s actual input size.

title: A wrong guess for one sampled sequence can be rejected without summing it
impact: After two direct divisor checks, testing the odd-stride sequence reduces to powers of units. A failing power certifies failure at that specific starting offset.
scope: The reduction applies to odd primes p < q < 2p with the prescribed odd stride. It tests supplied guesses and relates the two shortest periods.
detail: At 221 the odd-stride sequence has period 24. Dividing by its common factor with the power of two removed from the stride gives 12, the shared period at stride 110.

title: A square-root test can find the primes before the first shared repeat
impact: On a constructed 2,048-bit product the square-root search split the number at guess 6. The shortest shared repeat, calculated from the recovered factors, had 2,043 bits.
scope: For distinct primes with 7 ≤ p < q ≤ 2p, the first correct square-root guess is the squarefree part of the shortest shared repeat. Finding that part cheaply for a general product remains open.
detail: The first guess is obtained by removing the largest square divisor from the repeat. We also characterize every later guess that recovers the sum. The 14,647 control was chosen for its square totient.

sources.label: Which period multiples recover the sum

title: One modular power can disprove a proposed shared repeat
impact: At 221, six steps repeat from one start. The remainder 118 from a single power of 3 proves six fails as a shared repeat.
scope: For two distinct primes at least seven and stride (N−1)/2, one failed test excludes the guess and all its divisors. A passing base can accept a wrong guess.
detail: Lean gives the exact fraction of units passing each guess. At length six exactly 96 of 192 units pass. Lengths 12 and 24 both pass for every unit.

title: Two reusable bases can test every proposed length
impact: At 221, bases 4 and 5 together accept exactly the multiples of 12. Two thirds of all ordered pairs there give correct answers to every guess.
scope: Two independently uniform units have a greater than 50% chance of being correct simultaneously for all guesses. Determining that a particular pair has this property is a separate task.
detail: The exact fraction is a product with one factor 1−1/ℓ² for each distinct prime ℓ dividing the shortest repeat. At 221 the factors for 2 and 3 give exactly two thirds.

title: A fixed list of small primes can settle a proposed repeat
impact: For a 2,048-bit product of two 1,024-bit primes, the prime bases through 2²¹ suffice to decide each shared-repeat guess under the published Dirichlet GRH estimate.
scope: The local proof takes a finite subgroup bound as a hypothesis. The cited paper supplies it under Dirichlet GRH. Selecting the shortest repeat is a separate search.
detail: A wrong guess has a proper subgroup of passing bases. The analytic result supplies a small prime outside that subgroup.

title: Even a trillion repeat guesses cover very few full-size products
impact: Fewer than one in 2⁹⁷⁸ eligible prime pairs has any positive shared repeat at most 2⁴⁰.
scope: The bound counts each sorted pair of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product once. It applies to the size of the shared repeat at stride (N−1)/2.
detail: The shortest length is a product of two coprime reduced predecessors. If it is small, both predecessors must lie in a short interval that can be counted explicitly.

title: One sampled sequence can encode the sum of balanced primes
impact: At 3,053, changing the stride shortened the repeat from 105 to 15 and gave the sum 114. At 221, removing a power of two from the stride corrected a misleading six-step repeat.
scope: For odd primes p < q < 2p, two direct divisor checks cover the exceptional cases. In the rest the exact shortest repeat at the specified odd stride gives the sum.
detail: Grouping terms reduced 77,070 updates to 210 at 3,053. Computing the groups still used all 3,053 residues, while Fermat's method found the same primes in two square tests.

sources.label: Lean proof for the single sequence

title: The shortest four-term rule determines the prime sum
impact: For 143 the shortest qualifying rule spans 11 even sums. Doubling the span and adding two gives 24, the sum of 11 and 13. Lean proves the general formula and its single exceptional ratio.
scope: The result applies to distinct same-width primes at least 11 and four invertible coefficients. The direct measurement on six small products used many sums. It encountered a factor earlier on all six.
detail: At 247 the exceptional span is 12 and the sum is 32. The quantity 24 × 247 + 1 is already the square of 77, which gives the factors 13 and 19 directly in this case.

title: Counting when two neighboring readings both vanish gives the prime sum
impact: At 77 there were exactly 19 such positions, giving the sum 18 and the factors 7 and 11. The same count at 221 gave 31 and recovered 13 and 17.
scope: The direct count takes one table entry per residue. Three related signs are easy to sample, but two fair coins and their product reproduce their distribution to within 2⁻⁹⁸⁰ over a trillion full-size draws.
detail: For every product of two distinct odd primes, the simultaneous-zero count is one plus their sum. We checked 526,786 positions across 276 small products.

title: The shortest recurrence for the even sums gives the larger prime exactly
impact: At 77 a rule reaching back four terms works forever, and every shorter rule fails. Doubling four and adding three gives the larger prime, 11.
scope: The formula works for any two distinct odd primes. For two 1,024-bit primes, the required order is at least 2¹⁰²². An inexpensive way to determine it from the product remains open.
detail: Eight even sums suffice to fit the rule at 77 if an order bound of four is supplied. The direct calculation of each sum uses all 77 residues.

sources.label: Lean exact order and finite-window proofs

title: At 77 the sums repeat after 30 degrees, exactly the unit-group exponent
impact: For primes at least seven, the smallest repeating shift gives the Carmichael function of their product. Taking only even degrees halves that period.
scope: The checker measured seven small products by summing every residue at successive degrees. Finding the period quickly from a large product remains open.
detail: The local sequence at prime 5 is constant. For 35 the even period is three, while half its Carmichael function is six.

sources.label: All seven measurements and the exceptions

title: Three terms can only compare even sums that already repeat
impact: For prime factors at least 11, every fixed three-term rule with invertible coefficients compares three identical values at different positions in the sequence.
scope: The rule must hold at every starting position. Its three offsets span at least two full periods. The distance between offsets is separate from the cost of evaluating a single sum.
detail: Four terms escape the restriction at 143. Offsets 0, 5, 6 and 11 satisfy an identity at every starting position, although the period is 30.

sources.label: Why sparse rules group their exponents

title: A fixed rule for predicting the even Jacobi sums must reach far back
impact: For 77, every fixed linear rule for all the even sums must reach back at least four terms. For two 1,024-bit primes the bound exceeds 2¹⁰²¹ terms.
scope: The bound applies to constant coefficients and a recurrence with leading coefficient one. Sparse long rules and direct ways to obtain a single chosen sum remain open.
detail: Even a rule that only fits the early even sums, before they reveal a prime, needs order at least floor((p − 3) / 4), where p is the smaller prime.

title: A trillion random signs look almost exactly like fair coin flips
